meta.regime: A week of flat, event-gated scores ended overnight and the board now has genuine two-notch spreads for the first time since the middle of August. Three central-bank inputs resolved in the same twelve hours and they resolved in opposite directions: the RBNZ delivered its hike and published a track too gradual to support the currency, Australia delivered a growth beat that lifted RBA September pricing to 57%, and euro-area inflation confirmed the ECB hike at 3.3%. Underneath all three sits the energy shock, which has re-accelerated hard - the US struck Iranian mine-laying capability directly and WTI is up 10.25% on the week - and which now transmits to every currency on this board through a different channel: terms of trade for CAD, imported inflation for EUR and GBP, an import-price drag for JPY, and nothing at all for CHF and gold, which continue to trade US real rates instead.

dailyRead: Three events cleared overnight, two of them resolved decisively, and for the first time in roughly two weeks this board has real two-notch spreads rather than a wall of currencies sitting at plus one. Start with New Zealand, because it is the cleanest lesson of the day. The RBNZ raised the OCR by 25 basis points to 2.75%, a second straight hike, exactly as priced and by consensus of the Committee. The kiwi then fell hard: NZD/USD is 0.58381, down 0.91% on the day and 1.78% on the week, through the 0.59 handle it had been defending. The reason is entirely in the published track, and yesterday's file flagged the right question while leaning the wrong way on the answer. The projection rises to roughly 2.6% in September, 2.8% in December, 3.0% in March 2027 and 3.1-3.2% by the middle of that year, with the eventual peak near 3.3% - materially the same profile as the May statement, and slower than a market that had been paying up for commitment. The Bank framed the 4.1% Q2 inflation print as largely fuel-driven from the Middle East conflict and said core inflation, wage growth and inflation expectations remain consistent with a return to the 1-3% band by mid-2027. That is a central bank explicitly looking through the energy shock, which is the opposite of what a currency long needs. Yesterday's file said a track implying 3.0% by December was a bid and a stop at 2.75% took the score to zero; the actual answer landed in between and the market voted. NZD is downgraded from +1 to 0, and the domestic data supports it - the manufacturing PMI COLLAPSED to 54.3 from 60.1, consumer confidence fell to 80.4 from 94.7, unemployment is 5.6% and business confidence slipped to 53.7. Australia went the other way in the same session. Q2 GDP printed +0.4% quarter on quarter against a +0.3% consensus, and annual growth came in at 2.1% against a 1.8% forecast, which is a clear beat even though the annual rate decelerated from 2.5% and ActionForex is right that domestic demand softened underneath while unit labour costs edged higher. The market read is unambiguous: RBA September hike pricing jumped to 57% from 48% beforehand. That matters more than the print itself, because the standing objection to the Aussie on this board has been that it had the best inflation case and the worst hike odds - the cash rate is the G10 high at 4.35% and the trimmed mean is stuck at 3.6%, but the meeting was only being paid 27-48%. At 57% that objection is gone and AUD is upgraded from +1 to +2. The euro is the third change and it is a correction of yesterday's call. This file argued that Germany at 2.9% and French HICP at 2.7% did not support the 3.3% area consensus and that the risk was a downside surprise. Euro-area flash HICP printed 3.3% exactly, up from 2.9% and the highest since September 2023, and markets moved from roughly 80% priced to FULLY pricing a 25 basis point hike to a 2.50% deposit rate on September 10. Commerzbank called the jump supportive of the hike; TE forecasts the main refinancing rate at 2.65% for that meeting, which is the same thing. So EUR is upgraded from +1 to +2. The caveat is real and belongs in the same paragraph: core inflation EASED to 2.4% from 2.5%, BELOW the 2.5% consensus, and services fell to 3.0%, with Eurostat noting explicitly that the energy surge did not immediately pass into underlying prices. Area unemployment also ticked UP to 6.4% from 6.3% and retail sales printed -0.3%. The composition still says this is likely the last hike of the cycle rather than the start of a run, and EUR/USD at 1.15799 is DOWN 0.11% today and 0.61% on the week, which tells you the euro is being outrun by the dollar even on a confirmed hike. Own the euro against the franc, the kiwi and sterling, not against the dollar. The dominant new fact on the board is energy, and it is a genuine escalation rather than a headline. On September 1 the US ran a large wave of strikes against Iranian targets - CENTCOM lists air defence sites, radar systems, maritime assets, communications and specifically MINE-LAYING capability - in retaliation for Tehran attempting to seed the Strait of Hormuz and for the weekend attack on the base in Jordan. Trump said an even bigger attack was waiting in the wings and that Iran would be hit at a much harder and higher level if it responded; Tasnim reported Iran had launched a decisive operation against US bases and interests in the region. That directly contradicts yesterday's file, which recorded Trump saying the response would be NARROW. It was not narrow. Crude moved accordingly: WTI jumped 5.2% on Tuesday, its biggest gain in five weeks, and is 90.722 this morning, up 0.56% today and 10.25% on the WEEK, with Brent 95.561, EU gas 73.54 euros and up 27.92% on the month, German gas 72.41, UK gas 178.29 pence and up 8.17% in a single session and 26.43% on the month, and coal 144.85. Transits through the Strait fell to 107 in the week to August 30 from 121 the week before. The FX transmission splits four ways and it is worth being precise about each. Canada is the direct beneficiary and holds +1 on a +3.3% annualised Q2, a revised-away Q1 contraction, capex +2.3% and now a 10% weekly move in its main export - but note carefully that USD/CAD is 1.39138 and UP 0.13%, so the loonie is not being paid for the oil move, which caps any upgrade before the Bank of Canada at 13:45Z. All 35 economists polled expect a seventh straight hold at 2.25%, there is no Monetary Policy Report at this meeting, and National Bank and Scotiabank both forecast hikes to 2.50% in October and 2.75% by December against Rabobank seeing nothing before Q2 2027. The statement language is the entire event, six days before C$27.6bn of retaliation lands on September 8. For the euro area and the UK the shock is imported inflation, which is hawkish for both central banks and a terms-of-trade hit at the same time - the DAX fell 0.4% to about 26,140 on Tuesday, the lowest since August 24, with energy-sensitive industrials, banks and autos worst hit. Sterling holds at 0: there was no new UK data, the annual GDP rate was revised up to 1.2% from 0.9%, and UK gas at +26.43% on the month keeps the administered-energy channel wide open into the October Ofgem cap, but the labour market is still soft with core CPI flat at 2.6%, wages at 4.1% and retail sales -0.5%. For Japan the shock is a straight import-price drag on an economy that buys nearly all its oil, and the Nikkei fell to 64,394 from 66,215. JPY holds at 0. The constructive side is that Takata, the July dissenter for 1.25%, spoke in Sapporo renewing his push for consecutive hikes and saying the economy has entered a new phase, which is exactly the signal yesterday's file said would repair the yen leg - but USD/JPY is 159.975, still on the line, still with no MoF response, and the intervention asymmetry above 160 has not changed. Keep it a range. The most informative observation is again the negative one, and it is now five tests deep: gold fell 2.3% on Tuesday and is 4,318.81, down 5.95% on the week, while the franc WEAKENED to 0.81261 on USD/CHF, up 0.88% on the week - both of them on the day the United States bombed Iranian air defences and Iran promised a decisive response. The haven complex is not pricing the Strait at all; it is pricing US real rates and a Fed at 66.4% for September 16. The honest wrinkle in the dollar story is that yesterday's US data actually MISSED - ISM manufacturing came in at 54.6 against a 55.2 consensus with prices paid flat at 71.1 rather than rising to 72, and JOLTS printed 7.271M against 7.3M - and the pricing barely moved, which tells you the market is now trading the energy-inflation channel rather than the activity data. USD holds at +1. Switzerland stays at 0 for a fifth session with CPI tomorrow at 06:30Z, consensus 0.5% against 0.4%, and note that Swiss annual GDP growth FELL to 0.3% from 1.1% even as the manufacturing PMI jumped to 57.1 from 53.2. The practical book today is the best it has been in two weeks: EUR/CHF, EUR/NZD, AUD/NZD and AUD/CHF are clean two-notch legs, sell the kiwi against the dollar and the loonie, sell sterling against the Aussie, stay long crude and short gold in size that respects a 10% weekly move, and take nothing new into 13:45Z.

Yesterday's file framed this as ASB's 3.3% peak against Westpac's expectation of equivocation and data dependence; Westpac was right. geopolitics: The war entered a sharply more kinetic phase overnight and it is now the dominant macro input on this board, ahead of any single central bank. The sequence matters. US forces struck two IRGC rocket launchers on Larak Island on Sunday after surveillance detected crews preparing to fire rockets loaded with sea mines toward the Strait of Hormuz; Iran retaliated against the US-operated base in Jordan. On September 1 the United States answered with what Trump described as large and powerful strikes, and CENTCOM confirmed a completed wave against Iranian air defence sites, radar systems, maritime assets and facilities, communications sites and - specifically - MINE-LAYING capability. Trump said the strikes were retaliation for Iran's failed attempt to add sea mines to the Strait and for the attack on the base, warned that Tehran would be hit at a much harder and higher level if it responded, and said an even bigger attack was waiting in the wings. Iran's Tasnim agency reported that the armed forces had launched a decisive operation and that US bases and interests across the region would be targeted by missiles and drones. This is a direct correction to yesterday's file, which recorded Trump saying the military response would be NARROW. It was not narrow, and the price action confirms it: WTI jumped 5.2% on Tuesday, its biggest single-day gain in five weeks, and trades 90.722 this morning, up 10.25% on the WEEK; Brent is 95.561 and up 9.80%; European TTF gas 73.54 euros and up 11.83% on the week and 27.92% on the month; German gas 72.41; UK gas 178.29 pence, up 8.17% in a single session and 26.43% on the month; coal 144.85 and up 10.03%; coking coal 282.00 and up 20.26%. Transits through the Strait fell to 107 in the week to August 30 from 121 the week before, so physical disruption is compounding the risk premium rather than merely threatening it. The FX transmission now splits four ways and each channel is worth naming precisely. Canada is the direct beneficiary and holds +1 - but the useful observation is a negative one: USD/CAD is 1.39138 and ROSE 0.13% on a day crude gained 10% for the week, which means the market is discounting the terms-of-trade gain against the C$27.6bn tariff wall landing on September 8, and that is why CAD was not upgraded alongside the oil. For the euro area and the United Kingdom the shock arrives as imported inflation, which is hawkish for both central banks and a terms-of-trade hit to both economies at the same time. It is the proximate cause of the 3.3% euro-area HICP print that took the September ECB hike from roughly 80% priced to fully priced, and of the October Ofgem cap rising 3.6% to 1,723 pounds in the UK - and simultaneously of the DAX falling 0.4% to about 26,140 on Tuesday, the lowest since August 24, with energy-sensitive industrials, banks and autos worst hit. Note carefully that euro-area CORE inflation eased to 2.4% while headline surged, and Eurostat said explicitly that the energy surge did not immediately pass through to underlying prices - so the shock is producing exactly the headline the Council said it would look through, even as it forces the hike. For Japan the channel is a straight import-price and terms-of-trade drag on an economy that buys nearly all of its oil abroad: the trade balance is MINUS 634 billion yen, the current account swung to MINUS 923 billion and the Nikkei fell to 64,394 from 66,215. And the most informative observation remains the negative one, now five tests deep and the last of them decisive. On the day the United States bombed Iranian air defences and Iran publicly promised a decisive military response, GOLD FELL 2.3% to 4,318.81 and the Swiss franc WEAKENED, with USD/CHF rising to 0.81261. Silver did the same, down 5.93% on the week. The haven complex is not pricing the Strait at all - it is pricing US real rates and a Fed that CME FedWatch puts at 66.4% for September 16, a level that held even after ISM manufacturing missed at 54.6 and JOLTS missed at 7.271M. That is the single most important structural fact on this board: rising oil is now transmitting to FX as a rate-hike input, not as a risk-off input, which is why XAU stays a short, why the franc remains the funding currency of choice, and why the cleanest trades today are long the two currencies whose central banks are being forced to tighten by the shock - the euro and, for domestic reasons, the Australian dollar - against the two whose central banks have said they will look through it.
